speechtext:
[u'In one of his most amusing pages which at the same time is most pregnant with philosophy and creative imagination, Rabelais describes Master Gas-ter, the personification, of the stomach and of those appetites which to many are the very centre of the universe.	[DOT]
"I assure you," he says, "that when. Master \xa9aster gives a command the heavens tremble, the earth quakes. His command is uttered; it must be obeyed without delay, else death will ensue."
And Rabelais parades before us all Creation: men, animals of every description, the willing slaves of Master Gaster, eager to serve him. And the prodigious nomenclature of all these beings in bondage under the sway of the lower appetites, is interrupted, at regular intervals, by the words, *ever recurrent, like a sort of refrain: "and all for the stomach."
You readily discern, Mr. .Speaker, my reason for recalling this page of Rabelais'. The ,Caster of our political life is the Union (Government which holds out to its supporters the alluring promises' of power .and honour with, to boot, the gratification of their gluttonous appetites. The Ministry's partisans bow to the sceptre of this modern Gaster so as to remain in close proximity to the Pork Barrel; "'and all for the stomach," say we with Rabelais.

Before our very eyes the Tory-Conserva-tives with their former opponents; lay aside their hoary grudges and conclude an alliance with the antagonists they have always hated and always fought, they wanted to get into power, and to-day they are striving to remain there. They are under the thumb of Master Gaster who loosens the reins on their appetites: "and all for the stomach."
We behold former Nationalists who only yesterday were widely denouncing all they worship to-day, take their place at the manger and bury their heads in the feast: "and all for the stomach."
We see Liberals, unfaithful to their pledge trampling on their principles, forgetting the past, deaf to the voice of conscience- "a famished stomach cannot hear"-enter a morganatic alliance with the Tories and bow to the rule of Master Gaster, viz., of their selfish appetites: "and all for the stomach."
And you see wealthy capitalists, trust magnates, profiteers of every description, kowtow to the Union Government to Master Gaster: "and all for the stomach."
Aye, "all for the stomach;" the Union Government exists for nothing else.
The present Government, has become so discredited in the eyes of the people of this country that we are all at a loss to understand how it has managed to hold onto ofiiee thus far. Those who support it and help to keep it in power, in spite of the will of our people, harken only to the lust of power and to their appetites that crave satisfaction.
"All for the stomach." There in four words, you have the definition of the present Union Government. In those words, so full of Rabelaisian flavour, you have the origin anid the end of this Government; Master Gaster surrounded by the Unionists, insatiable Garga.ntuas.
The stomach has its tragedy. " There is a heroism of the stomach, .said Victor Hugo; and the Unionists believe they are heroes because they make their conscience and their principles subservient to their appetites.
Union Government is merely the representative of certain factions; hence it fears the judgment of the nation as a whole. The Government represents Imperialism more than Ganadianism, the manufacturer rather than the consumer, the profiteer in preference to the victimized masses of the people. That is not- what their country is asking for.' In the words of Gambetta: "Ideas create parties; interests create factions "
The explanation of the dignity and smooth ' running regularity of the constitutional regime in England for generations is undoubtedly to be found in the fact that the popular representatives were divided into two great. Parties, the Whigs and the Tories, each in turn being raised to power by the movements of public opinion under the moderating influence of the Crown. On the other hand if parliamentary government has often hung by only a hair's breadth in Spain aind Italy the reason is to be found in this mania for change which split up the great historical parties into insignificant personal cliques thus paving the way for anarchy.
We must chose one or the other of these iJ.wo systems. The Liberals prefer the method of government by powerful parties, parties not only in name, but founded o'n ' [DOT]''.early set forth opinion and a well-defined policy, and whose members willingly submit to the iron hand of discipline which is essential to true freedom. The tenets of the Liberal party, Mr. Speaker, are far above all those factions whose policies are guided solely bv their own private interests.
The Unionist group is something in the nature of a "crazy quilt"-I crave your indulgence for the expression, Mr. 'Speaker; it has none of the characteristics of a great political party. The Union Government- is well aware of its own weakness and with good cause from the judgment of the people whom it has -deceived and whom it is how trying to avoid.
The illustrious tutor of one the Dukes of Burgundy wras wont to admonish his pupil in these words: "Remember, my child that a King is made for his people, not. the people for their King."
Those responsible for the present maladministration of our suffering Canada's affairs have forgotten that governments ar-e made for the people and not the people for governments. Perhaps these Unionist gentlemen believe that this principle was destroyed in the awful upheaval of which the world has not, even yet, -seen the end. Let me tell them they are wrong. Like many -other ephemeral leaders they are due to learin that the multitude knows its rights as well as its duties -and that, in this new day the knell of absolutism in the conduct of affairs of state, has sounded.

speechtext:
The hon. member for
LTslet (Mr. Fafard) having opened his speech in English and closed it in English, I thought that I should show appreciation of that courtesy by opening my remarks in the language which falls with such melody from the lips of hon. gentlemen opposite, and I will endeavour to close my remarks in the same language. '
Notwithstanding the very violent remarks that were made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) in opposition to the Budget introduced by the Finance Minister (Sir Henry Drayton) I venture to express my general approval of that Budget, and I wish also to extend to the Finance Minister my congratulations on the ability, courage and candour which he displayed in introducing the Budget. I entirely commend him for removing the 5 per cent and 7J per cent special war tax or revenue tax; which tax was never intended for any other than revenue purposes. I can understand that with the pressing needs of the country for additional revenue there would be strong inclination on the part of the Government to retain that tax. But its retention would have been a great mistake and open to misinterpretation; furthermore, its removal clears the way for that general revision of the tariff which has been promised and which will come a little later. I also wish to commend the Finance Minister in that he is taking steps to raise his revenue by a tax on what may be regarded as luxuries,-at least, by a tax which will rest upon those who are most able to pay it.
The amendment introduced by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) starts out with finding fault with the Government for not having carried out an alleged promise of the ex-Finance Min-isted (Sir Thomas White) last year in regard to an inquiry which was to be made and followed by a revision of the tariff. The attitude of the member for Shelburne and Queen's in that regard is all the -more remarkable when we remember his attitude on tariff revisions in former years. If you refer to the Budget Speech delivered by the member for Shelburne and Queen's in 1904, you will find a reference to tariff revision in these words:
But, sir, though we speak of that as an outline of the method by which there might be a detailed tariff change, we have to consider the question of things as they are to-day. We desire to deal with certain tilings as they present themselves to us to-day; we desire to deal with matters of urgency, reserving the question of a more general and more detailed tariff revision until an early date-I would say, hopefully, next session, but at all events as soon as a proper inquiry can be made.
These remarks were uttered by the member for Shelburne and Queen's on June 7, 1904, when he was Finance Alinister of this country. I submit that in these remarks you have as distinct a promise of tariff revision as was made by the member for Leeds when Finance Alinister last year. No commission of inquiry was appointed

see him to-day. The hon. gentleman's course in the House is typical of his course in connection with fiscal matters; he moves somewhat in a circle. This fact was evidently recognized by the hon. member for Brome, who on the occasion to which I refer pictured the ship of state with the Acting Prime Minister the present member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White) as captain, who was being warned by the starboard watch and the .port watch. The hon. member then added these words:
Then approaches with swift tread the quartermaster from Shelburne and Queen's and he says: "Captain, I belong to neither the starboard nor to the port watch. I believe in party government, a party of one. I tender you, captain, my independent support until 1 consider it is time for me and my friends to unite and make you walk the plank.
To this statement the hon. member for Brome adds:
I do not know whether X can congratulate or commiserate the Acting Prime Minister, the captain of the ship, for the support he gets from the eloquent and revered quartermaster from Shelburne and Queen's.
L wonder just how much the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's thinks of the support which he gets now from .the hon. member for Brome in his amendment. That amendment of the hon. member for Brome on that occasion was opposed by all on this side of the House and, I think, by practically all of those who now sit in the .third party. I know it was opposed very strenuously by the hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. Clark), the hon. .member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). All of these gentlemen voted, and .many of .them spoke, .against the amendment. What was said by the hon. member for Marquette on that occasion? What reason did he give for opposing the amendment of the hon. member or Brome,-an amendment which was proposing many things that are found in the platform of the third party to-day? He said, as will be found on page 821 of Hansard:
If the amendment were accepted it would mean the overthrow of the Government and a general election, with all the necessary turmoil that would ensue	I say that it
would mean the plunging of the country into a general election and that is not desirable at this stage. It is wholly undesirable for several reasons, which I do not need to enumerate.
He charges the hon. member for Brome with having introduced a resolution for no other purpose than to embarrass the Government in carrying on the business of the country. Well, I wonder what he considers is the object of the hon. member for Shel-

burne and Queen's in the amendment which that hon. gentleman has moved to this Budget? Is it not for the purpose of embarrassing the Government in their conduct of the business of the country? If accepted will it not put the country into the turmoil of a general election? All the reasons for which he condemned the motion of the hon. member for Brome in March 1919 will apply with equal force to the condemnation of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's which I assume, he intends to support.
That amendment of the hon. member for Brome was moved in the first part of the session of 1919 and was taken exception to very strongly by the hon. gentlemen I have named, but on June 9, the great resoluter on the other side of the House, the hon. member for Brome, introduced another resolution, the terms of which were practically the same, in substance and principle, as the terms of .the amendment which he had proposed in March. Now ten weeks had passed since his former resolution had been condemned in unmeasured terms, but the hon. member for Marquette, the hon. member for Red Deer and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's had experienced a change of heart. A change had come over the spirit of their dreams in these ten weeks and these same hon. gentlemen who had charged the hon. member for Brome with trying to embarrass the Government, and with having introduced a motion for the purpose of trying to throw the country into the turmoil of an election, got up two and a half months later to support the second amendment just as strongly as they had condemned the amendment on the former occasion.
Let us refer to some remarks made by some of these hon. gentlemen when the first amendment was introduced in March. I refer to them because they are indicative of the opinions which were held at that time on fiscal matters. Take, for instance, the hon. member for Red Deer who, speaking in the House on the 25th March, 1919, said:
In the year 1896. the so-called Liberal party came into power in this country, and in 1897 they introduced some trifling reductions of the tariff, and put two or three articles of importance upon the free list. They also introduced the British preference, which was also a fairly substantial piece of tariff reduction, and then they went to sleep for ten years. That is not the way Mr. Gladstone tackled the tariff. For ten years, from 1897 to 1907, my hon, friend *
Referring on that occasion to the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) :

__who is so excited now-who says there is to
he no such thing as waiting-waited with absolute patience during that long term, because the tariff was practically passed over for ten years, and then it was-I was going to say tackled, but that would be an absurd misuse of language-flirted with again in the year 1907,
Well, what happened to the tariff in 1907? Absolutely trifling alterations were made to it, and in some cases, so far from following the example of Mr. Gladstone, the tariff was raised, in favour of those woollen goods about which my hon. friend is so anxious at the present moment.
Two months later the hon. member for Red Deer was raving in the wildest manner against the iniquity of having a duty on woollens in a climate like that of Canada. This shows the change in the position adopted by the hon. gentleman in the course of a few weeks. In the same debate the hon. gentleman made use of these words which I commend to hon. gentlemen opposite:
The manufacturers of Canada were told by some one high in the authority of the Liberal party on that day, that they were not hurt in the reciprocity agreement.
He was referring to the spring of 1911 and he says that at that time the manufacturers had been assured that they were not hurt and would not be hurt, by the reciprocity agreement. Let me quote a few more sentences from the hon. gentleman:
When one thinks of the fifteen years' record of the Liberals in power, which practically amounted to the tariff being untouched, and not proposed to be touched in any way worthy the name in the reciprocity agreement.
Again:
What patience they had in power compared with their eagerness and impetuosity when they are in Opposition.
I venture to s<ay that there has been no person in this House who has given evidence of the virtue and the fault to a greater degree than the hon. gentleman himself. He gave evidence of the virtue of patience when he sat in support of the hon. gentleman who was then Finance Minister, the present hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, and he is as impetuous as any youth in the eagerness of his demands now for tariff changes notwithstanding the condition in which the country is. Note these further words of the hon. gentleman:
And yet my hon. friends opposite have such confidence in their ability that they say, "In your very first Budget, within three months of peace being declared, we want you to make ten times as drastic tariff changes as we were able to do in fifteen years in the times of piping peace." Is that a reasonable proposition to bring before this country on a motion for going into Supply?
Two months later the hon. gentleman was taking that very course; the 'course which
he condemned in March he was willing to accept as the .proper course in June of the very same year.
If the hon. member for Red Deer were here I would like to ask him one or, two questions. I would like to ask him in regard to his own position on tariff matters and whether it has been as consistent as he would like the country to believe. I entered this House in 1908 'at the same time as the hon. member for Red
4 p.m. Deer, and I have no remembrance of a single occasion when the hon. gentleman ever did anything more *than quote Cobden, Bright, Peel, "Lord This" and "Duke That" in regard to free trade in tariff matters. The hon. gentleman talks about 'Gladstone-what would Gladstone do if he were here?-he talks about Peel and Cobden. Well, I venture to say that if any of these men who are mentioned as free traders in theory, and who might also be free traders in practice, were members of this House they wouldn't sit here for twelve years without going on record as having introduced at least one resolution proclaiming their convictions in regard to free trade. Yet during all the time that the hon. member for Red Deer has sat in this House he has never presented one single specific resolution along the free trade lines to test out the House in regard to the matters which he claims to have so much at heart.
Not only that, but may I refer you to what he said in this House in the month of April, 1909? You will find his words at page 4704 of Hansard of that date. He was discussing the tariff. The Budget had been brought down by the Minister of Finance, the present hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. The hon. member fox Red Deer got up and, after lauding to the skies the Finance Minister for his Budget, and after congratulating him on resisting the demands of the manufacturers, when, as a matter of fact the only changes made in the tariff of 1909 were changes in the interest of the manufacturers, he went on to use these words:
Whereas, under what I still claim is a revenue tariff, you have had a series of surpluses under the able administration of the Minister of Finance.
So that in 1909 the hon. member for Red Deer did not regard the tariff as a protective tariff. He says distinctly that it was not a protective tariff, but that it was a revenue tariff, and he reiterated his claim to that effect. Note these words, page 4717, Hansard :

Give them (the farmers) a chance in the markets of the world by keeping your tariff down to a revenue basis.
The hon. gentleman says "give them a chance"-give them a chance by keeping the revenue tariff not by having the tariff removed. He was then sitting here supporting the Government of which the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was Minister of Finance. Again in January, 1910, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) expressed himself as very well satisfied indeed with the way things were going. As a matter of fact, the hon. member when supporting the Government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was extremely patient. At that time apparently he was in no hurry for free trade, for he lauded the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) on every occasion when he brought down his Budget; and we have only to compare the tariff of that date with the tariff of 1894 to- see that there was very little difference between them, and1 no difference whatever so far as the protective principle was concerned, that principle having been ad*mit'ted, in practice at least, by both parties.
But while the course now advocated by the hon. member for Red Deer is along the line of wiping out entirely all duties, what course is being taken in England at the present time? I have here a clipping taken from the Montreal Star of May 22, signed by the well-known correspondent " Windermere," and having reference to the attitude of the British Government in regard to redeeming their election pledges to the farmers of Great Britain. He cables:
Their Agricultural Bill, now before the House of Commons, is of especial concern to Canada as the " Future granary of the Empire."
Taking the wheat prices of 1919 as a basis, the Bill established a guarantee of 68 shillings per quarter of 504 pounds weight for wheat, and 46 shillings per quarter of 336 pounds for oats. But as wages and the whole cost of production have greatly increased since 1919, the Bill decrees that the minimum prices for 1921 and subsequent years shall be fixed by three commissioners, and four years' notice is to be given before this system of guaranteed prices can be ended.
There is the attitude of the Government in free trade England towards the farmer. If that is not a protective measure, I do not understand what protection means.
May I also call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to one or two other features of British policy? What about the embargo on Canadian cattle; is not that protection? Why, if they placed a duty of $100 per head on the cattle we want to ship to that country, they could not exclude them any more

effectually. It is a drastic form of protection beyond all question. Then what about their attitude in regard to fixing the price of bacon? They have fixed a very low price for imported bacon, but no restrictions whatever have been placed on the home grown article; what is that but protection? I could mention many other articles of food on which there is a specific duty, and others on which there is an ad valorem duty, and those duties in many cases are very much higher than the duties we Impose. For instance, there is no duty on gasoline coming into Canada; there is a duty of 12 cents a gallon on gasoline imported into Great Britain. Our highest duty on coffee is 2 cents a pound; their duty is 6 cents a pound. Our duty on tea is 10 per cent, except where it is imported direct, when it is admitted free; their duty is 24 cents a pound. In addition they have duties on condensed milk, plums, prunes, raisins, cocoa, chicory, figs, molasses and other articles of food, all of which must be regarded as necessaries of life. And yet hon. gentlemen like the hon. member for Red Deer would have us believe that no duties are imposed in England, when as a matter of fact their customs and excise duties per head of population are pretty near double those imposed in this -country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to direct your attention to fiscal matters in 1909. In that year the Liberal party discovered a new star, and the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) entered this House as Minister of Labour. In 1910, under the direction of that hon. gentleman, a report was prepared on wholesale prices in Canada over a period of twenty years from 1890 to 1909. I would call particular attention to these words in the preface to that report:
For some time past, especially since the beginning of the present century, one of the most important features of the general economic situation in Canada has been a rapid and continuous advance in prices and the cost of living. When the history of 1910 comes to be written not the least memorable of its happenings to be chronicled will probably be the great agitation, partaking of the proportions of a national revolt, against the high prices of food.
I ask the House to note the concluding phrase:
-partaking of the proportions of a national revolt, against the high prices of food.

That is at the beginning of the report prepared at the instance of the present leader of the Opposition and sub-

mitted by him to the House and to the country with his approval. That is a very startling statement, Mr. Speaker-that the prices of food had risen to such a point in the Dominion that the people were on the point of revolting. That sentence is a rather severe comment on the praise which has been bestowed by certain gentlemen opposite on the conduct of affairs when they were in power. If, as is asserted so frequently by hon. gentlemen opposite, the remedy for excessive prices for manufactured goods is to remove all tariff walls, manifestly the way to bring down the high price of food is to open our doors to the surplus food products of the world. That is apparently what these gentlemen think.
In the report to which I have referred, which was prepared and presented to this House and the country in 1910 and which, it was said, was of great use to the negotiators who went to Washington to negotiate the reciprocity pact, 230 articles were considered. Of the 230 articles, 40 represented what the farmer sells and 190 represented things which he and others have to buy. 6o convincing wae that report that the Government of the day considered that it would be in the interests of Canada, in the interests of the farmers of Canada, to whom they were appealing for support, to take the duty entirely off the 40 articles that the farmer had to sell and leave it absolutely untouched on everything that he had to buy. That was the conclusion that was come to by them in 1911 in the reciprocity pact, and that is the argument that they are presenting to this House and to the country to-day. Yet they pretend, as do the little group who sit angularly to my right, that they are the friends of the farmers of this country. I want to place before you, Mr. 'Speaker, some of the prices which obtained at that time,-prices which the present leader of the Opposition said were so high that the people were on the point of revolution. I may add in passing that these figures show that on all except two articles the lowest price was obtained during the time that these hon. gentlemen were in power. But, Sir, what do we find? Again I direct your attention to the remarks in the preface to that report: that prices obtained by the farmers at that time had gone to such a pitch that in order to bring these agrarian plutocrats to their knees; in order to bring them to time; in order to stem the tide of revolution which was threatening on account of the high prices which were being obtained by the farmers, they made this proposal to throw the doors of Canada open to the surplus farm products of the world, at the same time compelling the farmer to continue to pay duty on everything that he had to buy. When butter rose to 22 cents a pound; when eggs were 16 cents a dozen and milk 15 cents a gallon, the dreams of the then Minister of Labour were disturbed by visions of the red flag of revolution. Something had to be done to bring things down to a reason-onable basis. Sixteen cents a dozen was far too much for a farmer to get for eggs; 22 cents was entirely too much for a farmer to get for a pound of butter. Why, it was preposterous; sixteen to eighteen cents a bag for potatoes-whoever heard tell of the like? Was there not every excuse for the people taking up arms in rebellion against that sort of thing? So my hon. friends proposed to open the doors of Canada and to admit an exportable surplus of 462,000,000 pounds of butter; to admit 256,000,000 dozen eggs in order to bring the price of this commodity down from 16 cents a dozen, and to let in 2,290,000,000 pounds of meat in order

to bring down the exorbitant price of meat. The farmers were getting too much for their cattle when they were selling them at $4.26 a hundredweight. They were getting an exorbitant price when they were selling sheep at $3.94 a hundred and hogs at $5.52-why, that was .an outrage indeed. Notwithstanding the fact that they had all these figures before them as to the prices obtaining at that time-these ridiculously low prices that the farmers were getting for their stuff, prices which meant that the farmers were leaving their lands because they were not able to make one-quarter of one per cent on their capital investment- notwithstanding all that, Sir, they proposed to open the doors of Canada to the surplus production of practically the whole world in order to bring down the prices that the farmers were obtaining for their produce. Yet these hon. gentlemen are obsessed with the idea that in the election of 1911 they were right and the people did not know what they were speaking about.

speechtext:
I had not the slightest intention of applying that term to the hon. member for Brome. What a useless waste of words it would be for me tp say anything reflecting on the mental calibre of the hon. member! He has given in this House instances enough of his mental capacity or incapacity, according to the way in which one looks at it. Why should I waste time referring to the mental capacity of the hon. member? I merely said that the trouble with these hon. gentlemen was that they still think that they were right and that the people were wrong in 1911, and that is a form of delusional insanity, the saddest

feature of which is that it is apparently incurable. If the hon. member for Brome thinks that is a reflection upon the gray matter which is inside that glistening dome of his, I can only express my extreme regret and pass on to the next point.
The hon. member for Brome would have us believe that he is an out-and-out free trader; at least, that is the line which he very frequently takes in this House. Is he an out-and-out free trader or is he under certain circumstances a very practical politician? Let us see what the Globe says in its issue of the 7th August, 1919, when it was reporting a very interesting occurrence which was taking place in Ottawa, namely, that last Liberal convention in which the hon. member for Brome held, I believe, the distinguished position of chairman of the resolution committee. One can readily understand why the hon, member was selected as chairman of the resolutions committee. He is the great "resoluter" of this House; he has been "resoluting" ever since he came into this House. True, he was put out of that little job this session, and I do not think he feels very comfortable about that. Another "resoluter" has taken the place formerly occupied by the hon. member for Brome. But on that occasion he was "resoluting" before that great convention, and this is what he is reported in the Globe to have said:
I have got to say that we must keep the tariff as an engine of raising revenue.
Voices-we have not.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Well, until you devise and put into successful operation some other scheme, I submit that you have got to.
Therefore, while in this House he does not propose any scheme, while he simply denounces protection, hip and thigh, and announces himself as an out-and-out free trader, still, when he was in convention with a number of other hon. gentlemen who were looking for and devising ways and means of getting into power, he then became the practical politician and said: "Well, it is all right for me to talk free trade in order to catch those who have that bee in their bonnet; but when the question comes down to a matter of practical politics, you have to have a tariff for revenue purposes; you cannot get along without it." That is the' position of the hon. member for Brome, and he is not the only one of that calibre on the other side of the House. We have the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), who declares himself as an out-and-out free trader. I am not very much disturbed by that, because

the hon. member for Assiniboia may any day get word from that committee of fifteen to become an out-and-out protectionist, and he may change his policy -when he gets the proper notification.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has been making speeches in various parts of this country; he wa3 particularly active around Ontario before the elections which took place last fall, and he has made certain statements which I am going to challenge, notwithstanding the assurance of the hon. member himself that he knows all about economics from A to Z. I am going to question his right to that claim and also some of the arguments which he has advanced from time to time in various parts of this country. The hon. member for Marquette has said that the tariff is the cause of rural depopulation. I might ask the hon. member to consider this proposition. Xf a protective tariff or a revenue tariff he the cause of rural depopulation, how does the hon. member account for rural depopulation in free-trade England? Or if his statement be correct that if the farmers of Ontario had access to the markets across the line, there would be no further migration of the farmers; if he be correct that free entrance to the American market would mean so much to our farmers, then I would like him to explain why it is that rural depopulation is going on in New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio and other States, just as it has been going on in this country. There are no tariffs between the state of New York and the state of Pennsylvania, nor between the cities of ,New York, Brooklyn, Pittsburg and other centres of population.
Why then is it that the rural population is leaving the farms if my hon. friend's contention be sound? The fact is that the rural population has been decreasing not only in this country but in every other country, and the tariff is not and cannot be said to be the reason for that rural depopulation. In the United States the rural population in 1890 was 63.9 per cent; in 1900, 59.5 per cent; and in 1910, 46.3 per cent; while in Canada in 1890, it was 68.1 per cent; in 1900, 62.4 per cent, and in 1910, 54.5 per cent. It is, I think, worth while noting that in each decade, with the exception of the state of Nevada, every state in the Union shows a decrease in the rural population. Speaking in this House in 1909, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), said that during the first eight months of that year, more people hai left the United States than had come
into that country, and he brought that forward as an argument against the principle of protection in the United States. If his argument in that regard was sound, I might use the same argument against free trade because of the people leaving the farms and country districts in free trade England. I might even produce as an illustrious example the hon. member for Red Deer himself, and ask why he and thousands of others have seen fit to leave free trade England where they would have all the advantages of farming under free trade conditions, and come voluntarily to the Dominion of Canada to farm in a country where they are hampered by protective tariffs or any other kind of a tariff. Why is it, if conditions here are as bad as the hon. member for Red Deer and -the hon. member for Marquette would have us believe, that we have people voluntarily leaving free trade Britain by the tens of thousands to take up farming in this country? Why have we people coming from the United States to farm in Canada? We certainly have very few people leaving Canada to farm in the United States, and we have no people leaving Canada to farm in England. That seems to me to indicate that conditions cannot be as bad in this country as these gentlemen would have us believe, and I am going to prove that. I want to say a few words more on this matter because of certain aspersions which have been cast on the province of Ontario and the farmers of Ontario by the hon. member for Marquette. I will not give the percentage of rural population in all of the provinces, but for the purpose of my argument I wish to give the percentage in Ontario. In 1891, the rural population was 61.2 per cent of the total population of the province, in 1901, 57-2 per cent, and in 1911, 47.4 per cent. In Michigan the percentage of rural population in 1890, was 65-1 per cent, in 1900, 61.7 per cent, and in 1910, 52-8 per cent. You will see from these figures that the percentage of rural population in Michigan is practically the same as in Ontario. Ontario and Michigan are very much alike in other respects. Farming, mining and lumbering are carried on in each, and there is practically the same number of farms in Michigan as in Ontario.
I would ask the members of the House to pay particular attention to the figures which I am going to give, and which I am giving because of certain statements which have been made at various times for political purposes by the hon. member for Marquette when he was endeavouring to influence the farmers of the province of On-

try, they have farmed1 them to a nicety, and I propose to show you how in some re-peets they have done so.
Take, for instance, the Grain Growers' Grain Company of (which the hon. member for Marquette is president drawing his salary of 815,000 a year, while the secretary of the same company draws a salary of
813,000,	the manager at Winnipeg a salary of 811,000, the manager at Calgary a salary of 85,200, and a young secretary a salary of $5,000 or an aggregate of nearly $50,000 a year. The first two or three members are farming the farmers to- some purpose. We had the hon. member for Marquette speaking in this House in June last year and referring to certain manufacturing establishments like Dominion Textiles, Monarch Knitting, and Canners Limited. He called attention to the fact that some of these companies were making as high as 31 per cent. He pictured in strong terms the iniquity of the whole thing and fastened it all upon the fact that we have a tariff in this country. Thirty one per cent! Let us see. The company of which he is the president in 1916 made $855,288 profit on their capital, or 62.2 per cent. Who said that? That is the sworn evidence of Mr. Rice Jones, secretary of the Grain Growers Grain Co., before 'the Costs of Living Committee of this House last June. In the year 1917 they made $844,401, or 44.9 per cent on their capital. This company was also handling machinery.

speechtext: Are these farmers?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
These are supposed to be the heaven-sent pleaders for the farmers interests in this country. They handled things such as binder twine, fence posts, fence wire and machinery of various kinds. What profit did they make out of machinery? In one year they made $272,215 or a profit of 21.6 per cent. Here we have these people, the tears running down their faces and falling in splashes on the floor in their sympathy for the farmers, ranting and raving against the iniquity of 12* per cent duty on harvesters. They figure out that 12* per cent on a $200 machine amounts to about $25 and these same gentlemen, through the operations of their own company, take about $40 out of the farmer on his binder. You would at least have thought that when it came to farm implements they would have handled them for nothing out of love for the farmer. Not so. They do not even give the farmer one hour of credit. They have no expense such as other firms have in connection with these matters. They sell for.

cash; there is no six or nine months' credit for them. Give us the cash and we will know what to do with it. We will pay it out first for the good salaries that some of us have the good fortune to receive.
Then there is another matter-the handling of elevator screenings. The average price for elevator screenings for six years up to 1919 was $8.84 but when the hon. member for Marquette was Minister of Agriculture he paid $35 a ton for screenings. The hon. member for Maple Creek(Mr. Maharg) came in there and I believe that I am right in saying that his company sold 1,600 tons to the Government and that there was a Government loss on the transaction as a result of buying these screenings of about $80,000. It is a wonderful interest they have in the farmers, is it not? They took these screenings and sold them to the farmers at $35 a ton.
Then there is the New York Export Company of which the hon. member for Marquette is also president. They had a profit, of $550,000 in one year on a capital investment of $250,000, or 220 per cent. There was only $100,000 of that capital actually paid up in cash. They had a profit of 220 per cent counting the capital at $250,000 and not $100,000 which was the actual amount of cash in the business, leaving out the water. Still we have these gentlemen, headed by the hon. member for Marquette, ranting and raving from one end of this country to the other about profiteers. They talk about what a terrible thing it is for a man to pay ninety cents on a barrel of apples ox a third of a cent on an apple. They are talking about profiteers making their millions but they do not call attention to their own overages in five years in their elevators of 357,000 bushels or $418,000 worth taken absolutely out of the pockets of the farmers. These are things which they do not particularly call attention to, for very obvious reasons.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that in the whole history of the two political parties that have held power in this country from Confederation down to the present time in dealing with manufacturing establishments of one kind or another-pampered industries, if you like, there has never been an instance where we have had such colossal and unscrupulous profiteers as the Grain Growers' Grain Company, presided over and represented by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. CreTar). It is the biggest profiteering' concern that ever was organized in the Dominion, and it is taking money right and left from the pockets of the farmers-those farmers whom its

members profess to take such a great interest in. And they take such, a great interest in the farmers for the reason 1 mentioned before,-'that they can "farm" .them, 'and they are doing it to tthe limit.
Why, Mr. Speaker, do you want another example of what 'they are doing along that line? Take what they did in regard to red clover, alsike and timothy seed. The "Farmers Sun" of March 13, 1920, contained an advertisement by the United Farmers' Co-operative Company, Limited, of Toronto, offering No. 1 red clover seed at $47 per bushel; No. 1 alsike at $41 per bushel; No. 2 timothy at $9.75 per bushel. Those seeds are not sold to the people as breakfast foods, they are sold to the farmers to sow; and those were the prices the United Farmers' Co-operative Company, Limited, was asking, and getting, from the farmers of Ontario. At Sussex, New Brunswick, is published "The Maritime Farmer," and the editor of that paper, taking an interest in farm organizations, proceeded to purchase the same grades of these seeds for disposal among the farmers and the agricultural societies as well as the branches of United Farmers of New Brunswick. After paying the freight from Toronto to Sussex, he sold No. 1 red clove r $4,450 cheaper per carload; alsike $3,550 cheaper per carload, and No. 2 timothy $1,365 cheaper per carload than these Toronto philanthropists were charging; or at the rate of $38.10 per bushel for No. 1 red clover as against $47 per bushel; $33.90 per bushel for No. 1 alsike as against $41 per bushel; 'and $7.56 per bushel for No. 2 timothy as against $9.75 per bushel charged by the aggregation in Toronto. We have, other instances. In my county a week or two ago the United Farmers' Company brought in a carload of seed potatoes from New Ontario, and they soaked the farmers $2 on every bag for just simply handling that carload. I say, Sir, that we are only beginning to turn over the leaves of this book which will demonstrate the truth of what I say, that the most colossal profiteering concern that has ever reared its head in this Dominion is that which is presided over by the hon. member who leads the third party triangularly across the way.
Now, Sir, there is not a member in this House who has less personal interest in manufacturing than I have; there is not a constituency which has less direct interest in manufacturing than my constituency. Up to the present moment there is not a single manufacturing establishment in the county 174
of Frontenac, unless we can so term a cheese factory. I could come to this House and denounce manufacturers as roundly as any hon. member without running much chance of hurting the feelings of the farmers of my county. But I take this position: I want to see manufactures in the Dominion, because so far as Ontario is concerned, at least, 90 per cent of all her farmers have to sell is sold at home. And I maintain that whether it be Ontario, Manitoba, or any other province, the best market for the Canadian farmer is his home market. That market I want to see retained and enlarged for him.
The 'trouble is that because of the very bigness of this country we are running into the danger of trying to legislate for this district and for that district, forgetting that if this is ever going to be a great country we must remember that we are members of the same family and must pull together. A little more team play is what we want. May I call the attention of hon. gentlemen from the West to one or two things which I will asik them to very carefully consider? In all seriousness I would ask them not to consider tariff matters entirely from the standpoint of the man who does nothing but produce wheat. I' might remind them that to the two old provinces of Ontario and Quebec must be given credit for 52 per cent of the value of our horses; 60 per cent of the value of our cattle; 70 per cent of the value of our sheep; and 80 per cent of the value of our swine sold. I would ask them to bear in mind that the farmers in these old provinces have diversified interests, and I would also ask them to seriously consider that we cannot build up this country by simply throwing open our doors and saying-Beoause we do not produce any fruit on the prairies, therefore we have no interest in the thousands of fruit farmers in Ontario, British Columbia and the other provinces who do produce fruit. We will never build up this country in that way. The trouble is that the representatives of the different provinces are inclined to act more as if they were the envoys of rival nations rather than the representatives of provinces which should ,be (brothers in the same family.
I repeat, (Mr. Speaker, that to my mind the most illogical and unfair proposition that could possibly be made is contained in this amendment and in the platform supported by hon. gentlemen opposite-a proposition which tells the farmers of this Dominion : You must climb tlhe tariff walls to get your stuff into other countries, but so



far as your own country is concerned, you will have to compete with the surplus products of the world. That is unfair, that is illogical, and if we carry that process far enough we are going to simply ruin this Dominion.
I wish to express my appreciation of the patient attention which hon. gentlemen have given to me, and I will do so by saying, merci beaucoup.

speechtext:
Bredner said last night-they are paid by the consumer. As regards clothing, 35 per cent plus 10 per cent, and as regards boots and shoes, 25 per cent plus 10 per cent is added on to the cost. My contention is that the excise duty should be paid by the manufacturer; it should be deducted by the manufacturer from the manufactured article and paid into the treasury at the time of the sale. Why could not that be done? On a $25 suit of clothes, the manufacturer would pay into the public treasury 10 per cent on the cost of the manufactured article, or $2.50. If you did not have an excise duty against the imported article, you would be absolutely all right; but having it against the domestic and also against the imported article gets you nowhere. If you would leave the tax off the imported article and charge it as a home excise duty which the manufacturer had to pay, he could not charge it up against the customer, and consequently he could not pass the tax along, because if he did, the importer would be able to sell his goods more cheaply than the home manufacturer. Therefore, the tax would necessarily have to come out of the manufacturer himself, and the consumer would be protected. Surely that is good doctrine. The Government recognize that policy themselves, because that is what they did this year in regard to patent medicines. Formerly, you bought a package of whatever it was and paid for it 25 cents, or whatever the cost might be. Under the stamp tax the vendor put a stamp on the package and the consumer paid 26 cents for the article. The Government recognized the fact that that was not good business, and now they make the manufacturer of the patent, medicine put a stamp on, and the manufacturer, not the consumer, pays the stamp tax. The policy is absolutely the same; if it is good in one case, why is it not good in another? I cannot see what the difference is, and I think what I have suggested is what ought to be done.
Some time ago in Montreal I advocated an excise tax to be paid by the manufacturer just in the manner that I have described. I argued then that the manufacturer had been a large profiteer during the war and that, therefore, he should pay, as he is best able to. My reasons are these. In the first place, this would save the consumer, and in the second, it would get back from the manufacturer some of the war profits which he had made. In England, there is talk of getting back some of "the war profits. Why should not a small portion of these war profits be taken from the manufacturer in the way I have [Mr. Pardee.1
eendeavoured to describe, and why should not the common man be saved that additional tax? By taking this tax from the manufacturer, we collect it >
from the man who is best able to pay, and that is what we want. Let us also remember that under these Budget proposals the tariff is left exactly as it was before; it has not been touched in any way whatever, and consequently the manufacturer is not hurt.

Patience is a virtue. 1 further stated in that speech that I suggested -what I did because I did not feel this country was yet ready for a full measure of direct taxation. That is the reason I spoke that way and it is the reason I am speaking that way here to-day. I have pointed out what I hope will be a constructive thought to the minister in raising revenue.
Now' let us turn to another phase of this tariff discussion, which is rather illuminating. The woollen textile industry, which has not been touched by this tariff, has a range of duty from 3 cents a pound specific duty to 30 per cent ad valorem, and it has a capital invested of $19,268,202. All these figures are taken from the Statistical Office. Its net profit was $3,578,318, or r8.41 per cent on its capital invested. Unitemized expenses, $1,107,126. The average wage paid to its employees-and I would call the attention of hon. members to this-was $624.04 per annum. The industry employs 2,530 males and 2,489 females, and operates 75 mills. That is a synopsis of the woollen textile industry.
The hosiery and knit goods industry has a capital invested of $31,092,866, and it made a net profit of $7,709,246, or 24.7 peT cent. The return shows "unitemized expenses," $1,715,847. What these "unitemized expenses" are is beyond my conception. It
has 108 plants, employing 9,000 females and 4,000 males. The average wage paid for 1918 is $516.32 per annum.
The cotton textile industry has a capital invested of $53,7%,394, and it made a net profit of $1,344,913, or 25.8 per cent. Again "unitemized expenses," $4,819,860. It operates 26 plants, employing 8,279 males and 7,725 females.. It has a protection of 35 per cent. The average wage paid is $538.23.
Now we come to the Canada Cottons, the statement for which was published in the Montreal Herald. The profits in 1917 amounted to $1,126,125, in 1918, $1,563,103, or 19 per cent, and in 1919 to $1,839,443. The surplus in 1919-1920 was $454,585, and their total surplus to-day is $2,683,479. The industry enjoys a duty of 20 to 32| per cent.
There is one striking thing about these figures, and it is this: Every one of these industries is manufacturing goods which are required by every man, woman and Child in this country. The industry enjoys a tremendous protection and is piling up surpluses every year. It pays enormous dividends to its stockholders, but if the figures I have given are correct the employees receive scarcely a living wage under conditions as they are to-day. I have often heard protection held up as the one thing that protects the workingman and gives him good wages, but here we have startling examples of what protection does not do in the way of giving working people a living wage. All these industries have a large protective duty, and it does not strike me that they are now altogether in swaddling clothes. The reason the protection is kept so high is this: The woollen textile industry, for instance, operates 75 mills; the cotton textile industry, 26 plants, and the hosiery and knit goods industry, 108 plants. Many of these plants are up to date, with the newest and best machinery and the best driving power that modern invention can give them. But some of them are weak sisters and have to be supported, and just as long as the weak sister is there, just so long you will find her willing to lean anywhere she can. Therefore it is that the people of this country have to dig down in their pockets and support the weaker plants in order that the whole combination may show a profit. That is the real reason w'hy the duty is kept where it is. It appears to me that is a remarkably good example of what a tremendously high protective duty does-it does not foster enterprises or advancement, but rather retards it.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries told us the other night at a little dinner that what this country needed was people, and ha

never spoke a truer word. I would ask my hon. friend how you are going to get more people in this country if you go on making the high cost of living still higher? Indeed, how are you going to keep those you already have here? Will people come to this country to-day with the high cost of living increased so tremendously by this Budget, and with your franchise law standing as it is? They will not. Now, you must have people in order to make a country great, and I would therefore suggest a different mode of taxation. In Great Britain there is a tax on wealth, a tax on property, a tax on all those surroundings where you find wealth. In Canada you have a tax on people; you have a tax on food, clothes and comforts; you have a tax on the man and his family. It is not right. It is not the way to get people to come to our shores. It is an absolutely fallacious proposition. The two systems of taxation differ as widely as possible. I think the Canadian people might well take a lesson from the British system.
Sir, I hope I fully realize the present position of this country. I know the country needs money; I know that we have to pay our way; I realize the fact that a country for which we sacrificed so much is worth still more sacrifice. But what is the best thing to do? I say again, that you must not drive people who have come to this country, away from the country, and you must not deter from coming those who want to come here. We must make the conditions in this country such that Canada will be a good place to live in. We have tremendous areas in this country which we must fill up with people and get them producing. I say, make a tariff for revenue, not for protection, have it properly adjusted, and I repeat, make the necessaries of life free. In following this course the Government, I humbly submit, would be doing something constructive. Get your money from those who are best able to pay, and thereby reduce the cost of living to the consumer. The manufacturers, I am sure, will be patriotic enough, indeed, they must be patrio-otic enough, to help pay the debt of the country which has protected them while they have been building up their business. The manufacturer, I am satisfied, will be patriotic enough if the Government is strong and forceful enough to reach him in the right way, and not be entirely subservient to the vested interests of the country.
In conclusion, Sir, I desire to say that I do not believe that the taxes proposed by this Budget will produce results. I think that with the complications and the machin-
[Mr. Pardee. 1
ery required to enforce it you will find that the retail stores will have tft largely increase their staffs, and if they are put under the necessity of having to pay more money to carry on business what will happen? Once more you will pile on to the consumer something extra which he will have to pay, and I do not think there is any question about that. For instance, apply this to such a firm as the T. Eaton 'Company. I was speaking to a large departmental store man the other day and he assured me that so far as he could see their staff would have to be largely augmented to carry out the tax provisions imposed by the. Minister of Finance. I have no doubt there will be all sorts of evasions of this tax. There will be thimblerigging in every conceivable way, and although I recognize the great ability of the Minister of Finance, I think it will require a far cleverer head than his if this tax is to be adequately collected. I am speaking with all seriousness. I believe, Sir, from what I can gather, from what I can hear amongst the retail merchants and amongst the people themselves in regard to the tax, that there will be evasions in every way which will largely augment the cost of goods while it brings no return to the treasury. Then if this increase is brought about, it means that once again the consumer will have to go down into his pocket to pay. So far as I can see, Mr. Speaker, this scheme will not, as the Minister of Finance hopes, prevent the abuse otf the tariff for the exploitation of the consumer; vastly otherwise will it prove, I think. Nor do I think that it will, in the words of the Minister:
Safeguard the interests of the Canadian people in the existing world struggle for commercial and industrial supremacy.

Then he asked the question: How is it that no great power, other than Great Britain, has adopted free trade? How long will it be, Mr. Speaker, before the population of Canada will be so large that it will consume eighty million bushels of wheat? I defy the hon. member to find in the Canada Grain Act, and frotm where else does he get his information unless it be from his associates? - Further, there are fifteen days' free storage in country elevators, and that includes not only the handling charges and storage charges, but fire insurance charges. Again, at the head of the Lakes, in the terminal elevator, ten days' free storage Is given before storage charges begin.
The hon. member also made a bitter attack on the farmers' organization, the United Grain Growers, Limited, for illegally taking grain from the farmers in the shape of overages. "Illegally taking," I interpret as stealing. In other words the hon. member claimed that the United Grain Growers, Limited, with other elevator concerns, were stealing grain from the farmers. Under the Canada Grain Act, as many hon. members in this House know, the operator of a terminal elevator has nothing whatever to do with the weighing of the grain either into or out of a public terminal elevator. A public wedghmaster, a Government official, is charged with the duty of weighing the grain in and weighing it out. A Government grain inspector is stationed at Winnipeg; all grain coming through Winnipeg is inspected and the dockage fixed. If needs be, the grain is reinspected at the head of the Lakes while it is being unloaded, and if a wrong dockage has been fixed, that is corrected. Moreover, while the grain is in process of being cleaned in the terminal ele-

vator, that operation is carried on under *the supervision of the inspector who puts the correct dockage on it. How then can any hon. member in this House state such a deliberate falsehood?
