subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I withdraw the statement. I am sorry that the statement made by the hon. member caused me to make this break. I appreciate your ruling, Sir.
Moreover, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) made a serious charge against the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster).
Speaking in this House on May 20, he said (Hansard 1920, page 2676):
Not only that; they induced the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make an amendment to the Grain Act which legalized what had up to that time been an illegal act.
Mr. Speaker, it is not for me to complain of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I pass on.
In the western grain trade we have three farmers' organizations doing a very large business. One is the company that has been under fire here for the last few days, the United Grain Growers, Limited, another, which is purely a farmers' organization, is the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevators Limited, and the third, also a farmers' organization, but not of this country, is the Scottish Co-operative Wholesale Society. This latter organization buys millions of bushels of wheat from Canada every year and does business, not with a single eye to making a profit, but to give service to their people, and its policy is to narrow down the margin of profit as closely as is consistent with sound business. Now when these two farmers' organizations of which I have spoken belonging to Canada are doing business right alongside this Scottish Cooperative Wholesale Society, is it possible that we could be such a rotten, corrupt, profiteering company as was stated the other evening by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens)?
I also wish to refer to some statements made the other evening by my good friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey). He told the House that Washington apples of a low grade were being dumped on the prairies to feed the poor people. He said in effect that this extra duty of 30 cents a box, for it
is an extra duty because there was already a tariff on apples, had saved the situation for the British Columbia fruit growers and for the farmers on the prairies, because it gave them a cheap and sure supply of good fruit and prevented the Yankees from flooding our country with apples, putting the British Columbia fruit grower out of business and then raising the price on us. But, Mr. Speaker, the people on the prairies have not found that cheap fruit which.the hon. member for Fraser Valley speaks of. We have noticed no reduction in the price of apples, but we have noticed an increase. That is only natural, of course. The British Columbia fruit grower, like the rest of us, is only human, very human. My good friend told us further that he was not talking politics, and I am sure we all believed him. He was talking money. Every box of apples meant an extra 30 cents in his pocket. In speaking of his loyalty to his country and of the huge debt which this country has to bear and pay, he said in effect: I am an old man, but I am prepared to do my share. He took very good care, however, to say in the first place that he rc juired his 30 cents extra a box on apples, and after he got that, he would do his bit and pay his share of the debt. But who pays the 30 cents duty on his box of apples. It is the poor people or- the prairies that he speaks of who are being fed on cheap apples from Washington. As I said, his loyalty to his country is based on the condition of 30 cents extra duty on a box of apples. Now let me apply to that the recipe of my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion), who said the other evening that if a little free trade was good, why not have complete free trade, or as he very aptly put it, as a medical man, if a certain quantity of strychnine and a teaspoonful of brandy was good for the heart, why not a pound of strychnine and a keg of brandy? Then why is my hon. friend from Fraser Valley content with 30 cents a box on apples? Why not make it $5. If one is good, the other would be better. While my good friend was speaking of fruit growing in the Fraser River Valley and of the splendid success the growers were having under protection, I could not help thinking of the poor people who live on the prairies who have hard scratching to get "an apple, and I was reminded of that little verse of Burns:
O wad some power the giftie gie us.
To see oursels as others see us!
It wad frae monie a blunder free us,
And foolish notion.

Now I come to the Budget itself, and I am glad to see the Minister of Finance right opposite me here. It is said that Scotchmen never throw bouquets, and I am not going to throw any I am just going to talk plain facts. I believe, Sir, that when the present Minister of Finance took office as minister of his department he adopted, with that strong personality of his, an orphan child which nobody else wanted. I say with all due respect that I believe when he came into office he had to handle the most difficult financial situation confronting this country in the last five years, because when he took office the treasury was empty. It was useless to try and borrow money outside of Canada, and the enthusiasm of our own people had waned somewhat. As I heard many of them say "The war is over. We have won our objective. Surely the Government will not want to borrow any more money." So with the treasury empty and no market in which to borrow, the Minister of Finance had to tackle a pretty stiff job. I remember meeting him in Winnipeg last fall when he was starting on his campaign in the West. The building where the meeting was held was cold. Winter had set in very early in the West and snow had come ear'ier than ever recorded before. A great percentage of the root crop was frozen in, and thousands of acres of heavy crop was snowed in and could not be threshed until the following spring. The dried out areas has suffered a greater loss than eve-before in the history of the West. Such a condition of affairs was not encouraging to a man starting out to borrow money. Not only that; the people bad pronounced against issuing any more Government bonds exempt from taxation. Then my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was practically compelled to go to a people who, I was going to say were unwilling, but many of whom at any rate were unable, .to lend any money. When I saw the horn, gentleman address that meeting in Winnipeg in a cold building in which people were sitting with their overcoats on, I said to a friend who was sitting next me: "What do you think of the prospects? What do you think of this, the first step of the new Finance Minister?" My friend replied: "Well, I wish him luck." After the meeting, as *we were going to the hotel, my friend said to me: "Reid, what do you think of the new Minister of Finance?" I said to my brother Scot: "It seems to me that the man who had courage to tackle the job in the first place will come through with this Victory Loan drive." I say, all 
honour to our worthy Finance Minister; but the position could have been made much easier for him if. when the war was on and huge contracts were being made with excessively large profits accruing from them, and when money was in abundance, his predecessor had taken time by the forelock and secured some of that money. This was not done, however. Nevertheless, I will take off my hat to a man of such courage and of such (frankness as I have seen the minister display.
Now, I come to the principle embodied m the Budget. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the principle of income taxation which was introduced by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) is a principle which is embodied in the plaitform of the Progressives. I am glad also to observe that the Budget contains the principle of a direct tax on luxuries. I am (in hearty accord with that principle of the Budget, Mr. Speaker, and speaking for myself, and I believe for the other members of this little group, this "contemptible little army," I shall be only too glad to see this or any other government embody in their programme every plank of the Farmers' platform. But while the principle is correct, in my opinion, I believe it is wrong in its application. I want the Minister of Finance to understand that I am putting forward my views on matters of finance as an amateur, but I believe that the principle is wrongly applied. I 'think that the scale of luxuries comes down a little too far, and perhaps it is not sharply enough graduated as it goes up. I think my hon. friend should have had courage enough to go a step further, and I wish he had read carefully the platform of the organized farmers. I should like to see every article which is made in Canada and which enjoys a protective tariff subject to an excise tax, and that excise tax should be graded according to the height of the tariff wall. Just let me read an extract from this little platform of ours:
That all corporations engaged in the manufacture of products protected by the customs tariff be obliged to publish annually comprehensive and accurate statements of their earnings.
That every claim for tariff protection by any industry should be heard publicly before a special committee of Parliament.
I claim that any corporation in the Dominion of Canada enjoying the benefit1, of a protective tariff should pay and should be willing to pay an excise duty to the Government, because it is our information- the organized farmers have delved rather carefully into this matter-that unde: the

protective tariff, before the treasury gets one dollar the manufacturer gets three dollars ; and I certainly believe that the excise tax is at least one way of getting pan of that three dollars which justly belong'- to the Federal Treasury. Furthermore, 1 believe that all the necessities of life should be on the free list, and the application of that principle would touch the great mass of consumers. Surely no one will condemn a luxury tax if it is not levied on things that are not really luxuries. Those who are able to afford luxuries should be satisfied to pay their share out of 'the large riches which they have enjoyed freely -for many years. We also have another little paragraph in our platform, and I trust hon. membeTS will pardon me for referring so often to that platform. I have a word to say for the disabled s-oldiers. I have mentioned this matter on the floor of the House before, and if I remember correctly the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), when sitting as chairman of the committee considering the subject of further gratuities to soldiers, mad' the statement that the Government would employ insurance actuaries to make inouiry into the advisability of establishing a life insurance bureau for returned soldiers. Now, this is the paragraph which I have reference to:	-
That provision should be made tor insurance at the public expense of unpensioned men who have become undesirable insurance risks while in the service.
I find that a great many soldiers did not carry life insurance before they enlisted, and many of them to-day cannot obtain insurance at any price. Some of them may be able to obtain life insurance, but at rates that are altogether prohibitive. I am still of the opinion that this Government should establish a life insurance bureau for soldiers, and if it were run under proper management it would not involve very much expense to the country. I was told by an eminent physician who had examined many of the soldiers that had been turned down by straight life insurance companies, that a large percentage of these men were quite likely to live to a good old age, but some disability or other prevented them from getting life insurance. I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is the duty of the Government to take some action in this matter.
I come now to the question of railways. The people of Canada to-day own some 22,000 miles of railway, and we do not need to discuss the question whether or not the
Government adopted public ownership on principle as being in the interests of the country. At any rate, the matter was t! rust upon the Government; there was no other alternative. Now, some people to-day are advocating a sharp increase in railway rates, and I am going to state my position to-night so far as this question is concerned. I -for one do not believe that the time is ripe for this Government to permit any increase in railway rates, for reasons vh.ch I shall state. All the people of Canada are to blame for the railway muddle which we find ourselves in to-day, and it is my opinion that we have paid too much for our w'histle. We have paid too much :ir the railways which we have had thrust upoi us. The next thing that this Government can do, and do as speedily as possible, is to make a physical valuation of the railways in their possession, such valuation to be made by competent railway men and to be made from the operating point of view. Then, depreciate the system to what it is worth and forget the balance. If it is under competent management-and I am not saying one word against the present management-and if that management is divorced from politics entirely you .should say to the men in charge of the systems: "We will supply you with the Tolling stock and necessary equipments and you must compete." Then, after .a thorough trial, if we find that our roads cannot pay under existing rates, it will then be time to raise the rates. I am convinced that in a very few years' time, by a proper amalgamation of all the systems of roads which we now have under our management, they would showf a profit and foe able to pay their w'ay. I make these remarks for what they may be worth, and I hope that the Minister of Finance will think over them at least.
Immigration must go hand in hand with our railway system. We have been bringing immigrants to Canada and putting them out West. It has -been our experience that many of our immigrants had not money to buy land and therefore they had to go back from the railways a distance of twenty or thirty miles. Grain cannot be profitably raised at that distance from a railway. Railway branch lines must follow settlement, and if we are to bring immigrants to Canada and encourage men to go upon the land, we must follow them up with our branch lines of railways so as to put them in a position to ship their products to market. I am convinced that if a proper policy is followed out, if branch lines are built and living conditions are made pleasanter -for those who settle upon the prairies

our surplus production of wheat will soon be swelled to the extent of many millions of bushels.
That brings to my mind the Hudson Bay railway. In 1882, when I came to the city of Winnipeg, I had my first experience in a federal election. Placards announced that Captain Scott "Is the man who will build the Hudson Bay railway." From 1882 down to the present time the building of the Hudson Bay railway has been made a political football. I wonder when this Government will finish the few hundred miles of steel that requires to be laid to the Bay. Our worthy Cabinet ministers tell us that the Government is committed to the project, but if they do not hurry up a good deal of the project will not be there when they come to look for it. It is rotting away. It is not finished, although it has been in course of construction now for ten years. Do not think for a minute that the people of the West have forgotten it. I hold in my hand a telegram from the Yorkton Board of Trade. In Yorkton to-day there is a large wholesale centre, and in the Board of Trade they have a good many farmer members. This is the wire they sent me:
March 29, 1920.
The Yorkton Board of Trade has passed the following resolution: Be it resolved that the Yorkton Board of Trade request the Federal Government to issue 20-year bonds to the extent of $5,000,000 for completion of Hudson Bay railroad, which shall include the amount required to complete the gap of sixty-eight miles between the towns of Sturgis and Hudson Bay Junction, to be known as the Hudson Bay main line completion issue, which bonds can he disposed of in Western Canada in a reasonable time after the issue is authorized on the basis of the Victory Loan.
Secretary, J. M. Clark.
I read that telegram to show the House that the people of the West will not sit down quietly until this road is completed. It is a necessity to-day, and as the years go by the need will 'become stronger. I wish to give you a few figures on the last increase in freight as it affects the farmer. The recent 15 per cent increase in railway freight rates falls more heavily on the farmer and the rural population than upon any other section of the community. It takes the farmer living in Manitoba an extra $14.50 on eveTy car of wheat-that is quite a chunk; on every car of oats $13.60 extra; on every car of barley $13.40 extra; on every car of flax the same amount. And it gets him again the other way when shipping in his machinery and other things that he must have on his farm. Therefore I claim that this proposed advance should not be made.

With the indulgence of the House I will give a few figures to show how the tariff works out at the present time, and I will take for the purpose of my comparisons the years 1915 and 1920. I shall make my comparisons in dollars and cents, as that is a pretty sure way of knowing what one is doing, whereas percentages sometimes do not mean very much. On a 14-inch gang plough the customs tariff in 1915 was $11.20, to-day it is $13.97; on a disc harrow in 1915 it was $5.03, to-day it is $6.34; on a shoe drill in 1915 it was $17.75, to-day it is $19.40; on a gas engine of li horse-power in 1915 it was $8.80, to-day it is $14.61; on a 5-foot mower in 1915 it was $5.60, to-day it is $9.50; on a wagon in 1915 it was $7, to-day it is $20.25. The percentage on the tariff works out very satisfactorily for the manufacturer, for as the price of the article increases so also does the protective tariff increase, and consequently the users of machinery have no option but to pay not only the increased price, but also the increased tariff.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make reference to an attempt which was recently made to muzzle the press of Canada, particularly the agricultural press. I am reading from the Grain Growers' Guide of March 17 of this year, the article being headed, " Moulding the moulders of public opinion." The originator of the scheme is Mr. G. M. Murray, .former general manager of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. The article proceeds:
The plot is as follows:	Mr. Murray has organized a bureau-presumably a Moulding Bureau-with himself as the Moulder-in-Chief. The Moulder and his staff are located on the ninth floor of the C.P.R. building in Toronto, close by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association headquarters. . Just what is the relationship existing between the Moulding Bureau and the C.M.A. doth not yet appear. But at any rate Mr. Murray has quite a staff in his Moulding Bureau, and they are busy reading and clipping papers from all over Canada.
When the editorial articles have been clipped then they go presumably to the Moulder-inChief, himself, Mr. G. M. Murray. According to his contract he classifies them and makes up his " black list " and his " white list." He then sends out his " confidential " report to all the Divine Right protected manufacturers who have paid him $250 per year, or more, to become members of his Moulding Bureau. In his " black list " Mr. Murray, of course, names those newspapers and journals who have dared to lay unholy hands upon the sacred edifice of the Protective Tariff. He then, presumably, advises the manufacturers-who have each paid him $250, or more, to join his Moulding Bureau- that they should' withdraw their advertisement from those offending journals.
Mr. Murray calls this scheme " shepherding advertising"'-Mr. Murray, of course, being the

Shepherd, and the low tariff press being the lambs to be fleeced. The Grain Growers' Guide was, of course, the most unruly and wayward lamb on the Shepherd's list and was to be plucked without mercy. All these journalistic lambs were to be fleeced of their advertisements until they would eat out of Shepherd Murray's hand and " baa-aa-aa " plaintively to be restored again to favour in the eyes of the Moulder-in-Chief and his battalion of Divine Righter protectionists.
But the tables are turning. The lambs have refused to be docile and have declared unanimously for the freedom of the press. The readers of the Grain Growers' Guide are ready to accept the challenge and are prepared to meet an advertising boycott by refusing to purchase goods from those firms who seek to cripple The Guide. Mr. Murray's plot has failed. He cannot secure a " safe and sane press " by " shepherding advertising patronage." The pitiless white light of publicity has exposed the rottenness of the scheme of this would-be Napoleon of the press. Instead of a bunch of journalistic lambs eating out of his hand he has merely caught a bunch of protectionist manufacturer suckers who have paid him their good money for an utterly worthless service. The press of Canada can never be bludgeoned into submission by any such Prussian methods.
I desire to also put on Hansard the contract sent out by Mr. Murray. It iis in this form:
The undersigned hereby employs G. M. Murray for a term of	
commencing	and ending	
(a) To ascertain by careful and systematic review, and to determine as correctly as he can, the editorial policy of every daily newspaper published in Canada (foreign language papers and papers published in the Yukon territory excepted) ;
<b) To ascertain by careful and systematic review', and to determine as correctly as he can, the editorial policies of such other Canadian publications as the undersigned may hereafter specify, or as said G. M. Murray may deem it wise in the interest of the undersigned to .embrace "within the scope of his investigations ;
(c)	To furnish information on record in his office or obtained w'ithin the period covered by this agreement concerning the editorial policy of any Canadian publication upon which the undersigned makes demand in writing for a report ;
(d)	To furnish without the formality of a demand In writing reports upon the editorial policies of such Canadian publications as, in his judgment, it is in the interest of the undersigned to receive;
(e)	To advise, with respect to any Canadian publication (except as aforesaid) carrying advertisements for the undersigned, as to the desirability of continuing, increasing, reducing or discontinuing the space used therein;
(f)	To advise, with respect to any Canadian publication not patronized by the undersigned for advertising purposes but apparently suitable therefor, as to the desirability of contracting for space therein ;
In consideration of the work to be performed and the service to be rendered the undersigned hereby agrees to pay G M. Murray the sum of	dollars ($	) at the commencement of the above-mentioned term.
It is further expressly agreed by the undersigned :
(1)	That all information, whether printed, written or verbal, furnished voluntarily or upon demand by G. M. Murray to the undersigned, shall be held in strict confidence, and shall never be revealed to the owners or officers of any publication reported upon, except in such cases and under such restrictions as may be authorized in writing by the said G. M. Murray.
(2)	That, while the said G. M. Murray undertakes to exercise good faith, due diligence and care in the performance of the duties herein specified, he does not guarantee the correctness of the information supplied, and shall not be liable in damages to the undersigned in respect thereof.
(3)	That the said G. M. Murray reserves the right to terminate this agreement at any time, by refunding to the undersigned the unearned portion of the above-mentioned consideration.
(4)	That upon the expiration of the term set forth herein, this agreement may be renewed l'or a like term by the undersigned again paying to G. M. (5)	That the duplicate of this agreement in the undersigned's possession shall be held in strict confidence, and that without the said G. M. Now, Mr. Speaker, my object in reading this-and it has taken me longer than I expected-is to shoiw this House that am attempt was made to muzzle the press of this country. The effect of that is well known to horn, members of this House. If the press is muzzled; if the press is trammelled ; if the freedom of the press is taken away, how are our people, especially those who live great distances from the capital and from the cities, to get the education and the information which is rightly theirs? I submit, Mr. Speaker, 'that this matter is worthy of investigation by the Government.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not very often that I take np

the valuable time of this House and I do not purpose doing so now. I have sat quietly here for .the past three sessions, intent upon hearing and if possible absorbing the views of 'those who have had more experience An 'the public affairs of this country than ilt is at all likely I shall ever have. While the hearing has been comparatively easy even at this great distance from the plaice where the stage is set in this House, and while I have benefited very greatly from the privilege of being here, in distant association with these great men, the process olf .absorption has been slow and somewhat difficult along some lines. It may be that At is to my discredit, but the fact remains that I find a.t this time, after ail 'the instruction I have received from prominent members on both sides of the House on the subject of the fiscal policy of this country, the convictions I brought in' with me when I first took my seat still hold fast, and, indeed, in some instances have gained strength to such an extent that I feel i't my duty-at this most propitious time-when the stress of war is over aind the country As rapidly settling down 'to a normal peace basis-to Diane my position fairly .and .squiarely before this House 'and before the people who have placed upon my shoulders the responsibility of representing .hem here.
In my opinion there have been many considerations An the past that needed careful weighing, and which were of much greater importance from a national standpoint than the possibility of being personally misunderstood, and I have not hesitated An meeting the criticism and even censure of those Ifor whom I have as great respect, and with whom I have more in common, than any other section of the people of this country, for the course 1 have followed in the past, believing that my actions were in the best interests of the nation, and that I have paid in some slight proportion at least, the debt of gratitude that is i due to those hon. gentlemen in .the Government who halve laboured earnestly and without consideration of sell in carrying this .country through the grave perils oif ,the last few years. I am satisfied that 'the future will show 'that they have done much to make the name of Canada famous, and that their names will be regarded by future generations as monuments to the tenacity and determination of 'a people who can never in the future be regarded lightly, but always as a power amongst the nations of the world.
Now, Mt. Speaker, the time has come when sentiment must be relegated to the

scrap heap, and we must get down to the serious consideration of the issues that face us in a more matter-of-fact manner.
Coming directly to the Budget, for I do not want to delay the House unnecessarily. There is much in the Budget that commends itself to me, and I think should commend itself to the country. The excise tax on luxuries and near luxuries is to be commended as a democratic measure which places the burden where it can easiest be borne. To that I have nothing but words of commendation with this one exception. Would it not have been better to have .placed this tax solely upon goods manufactured in Canada in the case of essential articles such as boots and shoes. I am merely using boots and shoes as an illustration and in no way singling them out for special treatment. When you put an excise tax on all hoots and shoes selling over a certain figure, the net result may lbe increased prices to thfe consume^' and the same old condition is perpetuated.
The manufacturer collects his profits, which a great many people in this country believe are very materially enhanced by reason of the tariff, and the real evil of a protective tariff still exists. Only a portion of the money paid by reason of the tariff goes into the treasury and the balance into the .pockets of those who manufacture and sell the goods.
On the other hand had the excise tax beeni placed upon goods of an essential nature having their origin in 'Canada only, we would have been able to collect the customs tariff on goods of foreign origin at the port of entry, and on Canadian goods by the excise tax. The price at which the foreign goods could be sold in Canada after paying the customs tariff would then have had a stabilizing effect upon the prices to the consumer. It is my opinion also that the application of a real excise tax to many other articles enjoying protection would yield a handsome revenue and would not work any real hardship on any one.
The system of taxation which is perpetuated by this (Budget, I do not agree with, and I can tell the hon. minister that it is not satisfactory to the great majority of the people in the portion of the country from which I come no matter to what party they claim allegiance. I would rather have the excise tax as it is suggested than not at all, but I merely wish to point out that the system of levying this tax could be greatly improved upon. As it stands the old system is perpetuated as practised by both the old parties, and this does not

meet the approval of those whom I have the honour to represent.
It was a source of keen disappointment to jne to find that no provision is made for placing such indispensible articles in the development of this country as farm machinery and building materials on the free list, or even the lowering of the duty thereon in a substantial manner. I have not heard any plausible argument put forward as to why this should not be done. The only hope we have is a' promise of a tariff revision in the future. I remember very distinctly hearing just such a promise made last year, and when called upon to do so, in defending my support of last year's Budget I explained that a tariff revision had been promised and that I considered the Government was entitled to be given the opportunity of laying before the country their tariff policy. I do not wish to be unfair to the Government in this regard. It may be that owing to the necessity of holding an extra session there was not sufficient time to do this work. But there surely was time to start it. This has not been done. What am I to tell these good people now? The only thing I could say is that a new minister has made the promise this yea*-and I am trying him out to see if he will keep his promise better than his predecessor. I have no intention of taking any such stand. It will take more than promises of future blessings to procure my support to Budgets in the future.
Even when the time comes and the tariff is revised. After listening to the discussion that has taken j lace during this debate, have we who do not believe in the principle of a protective tariff as practised in the past, any reason to suppose for one moment that there will be any downward revision or any change in the system of collecting the revenues accruing therefrom5 I think not.
Never have I seen such an acrobatic display as we have witnessed here in the last few days, on any other stage in the country. Members on both sides of the House have apparently been vieing with each other in vaulting gracefully and otherwise from one side to the other of the lines of thought on the fiscal policy. I am not offering any criticism of these hon. members. They have a perfect right to align themselves with the forces they believe will further to the greatest extent the interests of those whom they represent, always keeping in mind the welfare of the country as a whole, and I accept their action as being sincere. I ask 175
them to extend to me the same consideration.
An hon. member told us during the Budget debate of last session that we had at that time reached the parting of the ways. I did not agree with him then but I do believe that we hrve reached the crossroads now, .and I am sure that the changes of front that we have seen recently will prove that I am right in my conclusion.
I stated at the outset that I wanted to place my position fairly and squarely before this House. I stand four-square behind the tariff principles contained in the Farmers' platform.
To those who have seen fit to go to great pains to berate the farmers' activities, more particularly in the West, I have this to say: I am a farmer. I do not draw one cent of income from any other source except that eminating from the farm. I am a life member of the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, a shareholder in the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company, and this may be of more Interest to my hon. friends,^1 am a subscriber to the Farmers' Political Campaign Fund and heartily support the principle of raising campaign funds in this manner.
If these hon. gentlemen think that they have brought a blush of shame to my face by their efforts to show that there is something nationally wrong with my position as I have stated it, they are far wide of the mark. I consider myself just as true and just as loyal a Canadian as there is in this House, and they have only convinced me the more thoroughly that there is still abundant reason for the farmers continuing their efforts which were commenced when conditions were perhaps, more objectionable than they are to-day.
I do not wish to pre-judge, but I cannot see how I can support the tariff policy that any person must see will eventually be adopted by this party. An hon. minister has told us that- it is upon the fiscal policy that political thought-divides. I accept this as a statement of fact. I was elected to support this Government during the period of the war and demobilization. I have fulfilled my contract to the fullest extent and must now choose my path for the future.
I therefore purpose voting for the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, not because I think there is anything material in the amendment, but because I understand according to the rules of the House no other amendment can be moved and I have no choice in the matter.

speechtext:
As I have not that report I must be content with quoting from the report of the organization which I have just mentioned. I shall quote only a few lines, because I do not believe in the practice of reading long documents:
Of the extraordinary increase in the price of sugar now amounting to 300 per cent, the study says, the increase in labour cost paid by the consumer was less than 15 per cent. .	.	.In the meat packing industry, where profits were said to have increased between 300 and 400 per cent, the labour item was shown so small that a wage increase of 100 per cent would add less than five per cent to the total cost of the meat. .	.	.
Profits absorb approximately one-half the retail price of certain kinds of cloth, the report declared, while the labour item amounts to from one-fourteenth to one-twentieth of the price.
I shall nut read any further. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that, 'the farmers and the labour men are legitimate factors in the determination of prices, and the real profiteer is the man who stands between them, the middleman, the agent, the commission broker who produces nothing yet sells everything; who buys butter, eggs and vegetables from the farm and sells them back at exorbitant profits to the city people. In the transfer of produce from the place of production to the spot of consumption you
[Mr. Rinfret.l
have the whole process of profiteering. And the remedy must be applied at the source of the evil. In these days, from the moment when an egg' is laid by a good-willing hen to the moment this highly essential and venerable product appears in the china cup before the consumer, it has travelled such a long way that it has increased as much in price as it has lost in freshness. It is brought from the farm in a state of innocence. It is put into a box and placed on board train; then from the train it is taken to a cold storage, where it lies in long confinement and meditation. Later on it pays a visit to a wholesale house and is handled by quite a number of agents. Then it spends a few days in the slhop of the retailer at the street corner. Finally, after this extended tour, full of age and wisdom, it dies a natural death on the plate of the consumer. How many people, Mr. Speaker, from the poultry yard to tile breakfast table, have handled this product and, thereby increased its cost? There, Mr. Speaker, you have the whole question, if I dare say, in an eggshell. The high cost of these articles is due to useless manipulation and criminal abuse of cold storages, and it i3 just there that the Government should intervene. Let me say a few words in regard to cold storages. It is a well known fact that cold storage owners prefer to allow thousands of pounds of meat to perish rather than have the market flooded for fear that poor people might be able to obtain food at reasonable prices. These institutions were designed pre-eminently to store goods so that in the bad season they could be sold at cheap prices, but they have served the very opposite purpose. They have not been utilized as refrigerators for the food of the people but they have been nothing but closed vaults to aid in speculation. This Government should see that these cold storages are properly controlled as has been done in other countries. The Liberal party in the convention of August last saw to that point and placed in its programme a resolution from which I beg to quote the following paragraph:
With the object of reducing the high cost of living by eliminating as far as possible the waste and expense in handling food products between the producer and the consumer, it is expedient to extend the principle and system of Canadian Government elevators, and to provide interior and terminal cold storage warehouses equipped for the assembling, assorting, etc., of food.
I will quote no further. The Government says that the people should economize. I think. Sir, that by these new taxes they

are introducing it will be very hard for. the people to economize, because they will have no money left. I think that economy is akin to charity in this respect, that it ought to begin at home, and I would therefore ask the Government to economize. The Government, however, have brought down a Budget that shows us a sum of $550,000,000 which, they admit, they have revenue to cover only to the extent of two-thirds of that amount. Yet in the opening of the session in the Speech from the Throne this House was informed:
It is satisfactory to know that business in Panada has been well maintained, that production has been large, and that general conditions are on the whole satisfactory.
This is the kind of satisfaction that the Government has to offer the Canadian people. I do not wish to dwell at any length on the Budget, but I cannot but deplore the fact that the Government not only has been unable to relieve, but it has added very greatly, to the already heavy burden which the poor consumer such as the low salaried men, the clerks and labour men now have to bear. Not only does the Government not relieve that class of people, but they add to their burden. The Government say that they are going to tax luxuries.Well, that reminds me of the statement of an economist who claimed that there were only three things which were essential to human life, namely, a glass of water, a loaf of bread and a blanket. I think the Minister of Finance must have consulted that economist when framing his Budget, because he has taxed pretty nearly everything but water, bread and blankets.

As to these taxes, Mr. Speaker, I had occasion to visit my division during the holidays. That division happens to be an important one, and the fact that I am about to state may possibly not surprise the Government. Probably they expected it; if they did they have not been disappointed. These taxes ere damned hy every one, bolth by the merchants and by the purchasers. I could say much about these taxes but I will limit myself to a few words. It has been shown that these taxes will create a lot of confusion. I said a
moment ago that the Government taxed pretty nearly everything. That was a mistake. There are some oddities in this new taxation that the Minister of Finance has brought in. For instance, II do 'not know why it is that the Minister of Finance is taxing umbrellas when he is not taxing canes. ,1 suppose he would want to lay a burden on the man who is putting something aside for a rainy day. The Government is taxiing glassware but it is not taxing china. You may hot drink-I shall not say wine because wine is not to be touched these days-but you may not drink water in a piece of cut glassware because you will be taxed but if you choose to drink it in the highest grade of Dresden, Saxony and (Limoges ware you will be beyond the reach of the tax. Why the minister has done that no one can possibly know.

speechtext:
I will accept .the word of my hon. friend. It has already been shown that this tax will lead to fraud. I know there are stores-I will not admit they are in my own division-where they have already started imposing a tax on every line of goods no matter what the price may be. 1 also predict that before many months at will be practically impossible to buy a hat below $5 or a pair of shoes beloiw $9 or a suit of clothes below $45 because the inducement that is given by this system of taxation will be so great .that merchants will increase even low grade merchandise to the prices fixed by the Government.
With regard to the luxury tax, I might quote the Montreal Gazette which stated not later than this morning that it considered that .the Government had fixed the limit of price on clothes at too low an amount. The Gazette says:	.
He draws the taxation on clothing at the line not of luxury, but of necessity. It is not extravagance to-day to pay $45 for a suit of clothes, or $9 for a pair of boots.
With that I thoroughly agree. But there is also a general feeling that these taxes are altogether unfair. [DOT] I will give an example that was pointed out to me of how it will .affect the druggists. It relates to patent medicines. These medicines will be subject to four different taxes if they contain alcohol. They will first, have to pay $2 per gallon on alcohol: they will then have to .pay one per cent on the wholesale price; they will then have to pay for the stamps which must be affixed to the bottles and finally they will have to pay for the 39 per cent tax on patent medicines. The

Ottawa Journal refers to this point. I shall not quote from my own paper or from Liberal papers but I am going to quote the Ottawa Journal. It says:
Further consideration might well be given by the Government to this heavy tax on what has become a necessity in many families unable to bear it. Doubtless a remedy for pain oi discomfort is a luxury to the sick, "but it is hardly the kind of luxury that the public treasury should profit from. Besides which, the proposed tax is unfair because it hits only the liquid medicines.
There as another point about -this tax upon which merchants and the public at large ifeel very keenly and that is that the tax should be imposed not on the full amount but only on the excess of the amount over what the Government has determined. The other day, when my hon. triend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) made a speech, he claimed that in the United States this tax on luxuries wias charged only on the excess. He was 'Contradicted by some hon. member on the other side of the House who wanted to wager a hat that he was wrong. I am afraid my hon. friend will have to pick up the hat and I will quote from the United States revenue law hs approved on February 24, 1919. It reads thus:
Sec. 904 (a) That on and after May 1, 1919, there shall be levied, assessed, collected and paid a tax equivalent to 10 per centum of so much of the amount paid for any of the following articles, as in excess of the price hereinafter specified as to each such article, when such article is sold by or for a dealer or his estate on or after such date for consumption or use.
This makes the case very clear that the United States charge the tax only on the excess and not on the lull amount; so that my hon. friend from Brome was altogether light and he is entitled to receive the hat from my hon. friend on the other side.
But there is something more to be said about this tax. The Minister of Finance himself has no idea what will be the result of the tax. Speaking lo the Montreal Gazette on the 21st May he said:
There will, no doubt, be some confusion for a time," Sir Henry Drayton, Minister of Finance, remarked to-day, " but that is inevitable with any new methods of taxation. When the system begins to operate it will be found to work smoothly."
Let us hope that it will prove true.
The luxury taxes will accomplish one of two things-either they will provide revenue or they will bring down prices. Revenue is needed, but if the cost of living is reduced, we shall feel that the luxury tax has equally accomplished its purpose.
(Mr. Rinfret.]
That is what the Minister of Finance says. Just imagine if you were to go to a physician and he were to give you a bottle and say: "This may be good for your appetite, or it may be good for your stomach, or it may clear your liver or possibly you may use it as an ointment; at least try it any way; it will do you no harm." That is exactly the stand take.i by the Minister of Finance. But I will say to the Minister of Finance that there is another alternative that he has not foreseen in connection with this system. It may reduce the cost of living, it may produce revenue; but it may also lessen trade, as the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has said and it may put out of business quite a number of a certain class of retailers who will not be able to go on with their trade with this tax imposed on the special lines of goods which they are at present se'ling.
But the Government says that it needs revenue. It needs $50,000,000 a year for railways. But because it has seen fit to buy some railways, I think it is rather hard to impose taxes on everything our people wear because the Government blundered in that particular instance. The Government also needs revenue because at this time when we boast- that we are done with militarism the Government is still spending $12,000,000 a year on the Militia, which is many millions more than we thought of spending before the war and when we were preparing for it. The Government also needs revenue because in previous years it offered war loans to the extent of $1,380,000,000 free of taxation. I do not wish to be personal, but I will give an illustration in a general way of how this tax exemption works out. Suppose that a multi-millionaire-and I think it actually took place-invested $1,000,000 in those war loans, bringing him an income of $55,000 a year, for which investment at the time he would be praised for his "patriotism"; that income of $55,000 should have been more than cut in half and I suppose at least $30,000 should have gone into the public treasury in the form of income tax, but as a result of exempting those war loans from taxation that patriotic gentleman has made an investment against the public interest to the extent of some $30,000 a year.
But there is this further feature to be considered, Mr. Speaker. We are paying interest on a huge war debt, and if we look at it closely we shall find that this war debt not only comprises the expenses of the war proper, but it also comprises the huge profits which were made by some friends of the

Government during the war; in other words, we are paying interest on the large profits made by the friends of this Government, and those profits have been stored away safely in those tax-free war loans. Which means that to-day we are paying the interest on a large portion of those war profits; and while those privileged beings, friends of the Government, are in full enjoyment of their revenue, the Government is forced to tax the common people and to maintain a high tariff.
Naturally during this debate much has been said about the tariff, and reference has been made to the division which I represent. Before I come to that point, I would like to answer a question put by hon. gentlemen opposite who have occasionally asked us:	What would you do if
you were in our place? Well, we would be placed in the position of a tenant who enters a house that has been badly kept for a number of years. We would probably have to spend some money in papering the walls, repairing the floors, and possibly in fumigating some of the rooms. But should we enter that house, we would see to the fullest extent possible that the damages were paid for by the people who had caused1 the damage before we proceeded to administer the affairs of the country.
The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne)-who is not in his seat now-said that the election of St. James was waged and won on protection. I have Hansard before me, and I will, read a passage of his speech, because it sounds so new to me. He said:
My genial and astute friend, the member for Beauce (Mr. Boland) -
whenever there is a compliment paid to some hon. member on this side of this House we may be sure of what is going to follow.

who was doing all he could to elect the hon. memberthat is myself, and I feel much obliged to the member for Beauce.
-who now represents that great division in this House (Mr. Rinfret)-
you will notice, Sir, how my hon. friend was full of compliments before he reached his point.
-also made a very strong protectionist speech.
I will not take issue with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries if he has not been better informed on this election. As will be remembered, there was no straight Government candidate in the division, and therefore the information that my hon. friend
was able to collect was naturally from a .most indirect source. But if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is under the impression that the St. James election was won on a platform of protection, I must inform him that he is labouring under a delusion.
Last night the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) gave us a most spectacular performance; he was speaking behind heaps of books and documents, and during the course of his speech he culled extracts from those books and documents as a busy bee would gather honey from a bed of flowers. And he also was very free in putting questions to the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) until the latter could stand it no longer and left the Chamber. Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister was perfectly aware that we could not reply to his questions. He knows the rules of the House very well, and even if he had forgotten about them I know that the Chair would at once have recalled them. But he kept on putting questions to this side of the House and then looking to his supporters as if to pick applause f.om their very eyes, and again turning to us and saying, "The hon. gentlemen cannot answer my questions." But the hon. minister knew all the time that we were precluded from answering him Unfortunately he is not in his seat now, but if he were I would have felt like putting a few questions to him in turn. Of course, possibly I would not care for a reply, possibly I would like to put to his very lips the same chalice that he wanted us to dirink from last night. But just the saone I might have asked him why, after spending two hours in the afternoon to demonstrate that free trade has been a failure in England, and that the people there are gradually coming back to protection, he found it necessary to spend two more hours in the evening-and to what purpose, Mr. Speaker'

to show that this Government has on some items lowered the tariff even below the reciprocity point! And yet the hon. minister would put questions to us and look at us staringly as if he had silenced us forever.
I would like to ask what the hon. gentleman was arguing about all yesterday afternoon and last night; was he arguing protection, or was he arguing for a lower tariff? I think he was arguing both, Sir. It seemed to me that he could cut his speech in two, and senl the afternoon part about protection coming back into favour

in England to his frfencs at Toronto-if he has any ieft there; and the other part where he demonstrated that this Government has lowered the tariff even lower than reciprocity called for he might send to his western friends. And after the hon. minister had made those two demonstrations in one day, it will be remembered that he concluded by admonishing us always to be consistent when dealing with fiscal policy!
As to the St. James election, I desire to be very emphatic in stating that at every meeting we held we stood for a lowering of the tariff on food, we stood for the very piinciple that is embodied in the resolution of the Liberal party that was adopted in August last, and which was read on many occasions by various s/peagers during the campaign; and atlso for the principle embodied, for although less specific it is the same principle, in the amendment proposed the other day by my hon. friend for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding).
My hon. friends opposite say that -we are receding from former policies; that we are not consistent in the matter of fiscal policies. If this were a free trade country, I could quite understand hon. members opposite saying that in such an amendment as we are now supporting we were drawing backwards. But for a number of years we have had to deal with a high protective tariff. Everybody knows, even those, I think, /who argue to the contrary, that to step from that high tariff to plain, absolute free trade would be national suicide. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is indicated by the very processes of nature itself. When a man's limb has been bitten by frost and you wish to restore it to its natural warmth, you do not expose it at once to the heat of an oven or a fire; but, lest you would lose it, you friction it with snow so that life and blood will gradually return to the inert limb. That is what we are trying to do. We have to-day a cold and inert tariff. We all understand that, having regard to the welfare of the country, it would be a great mistake to expose it once to the open air. We wish to take a cautious, a prudent, a gradual step. The Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) made a pathetic-appeal to me yesterday to support the Budget because I had promised that to my electors. I am full aware of my responsibility, Mr. Speaker, as a public man, and I say that when I do vote for the amendment brought down by the member for Shelburne and Queen's I will fully meet the views of the whole electorate of St. James, because the 
labour .man who opposed me also stood for a moderate tariff.
There are other points that one would feel like touching upon, but I do not wish to overburden this House with speech. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), speaking of customs valuations, complained that the Government were having the goods valued on the basis of the nominal value of foreign money and were not taking into consideration the current rate of exchange. Tiiis is a veiy special matter upon which I have some documentation, and I think it would be better to leave it over; probably there will be an opportunity later in the session, or when we take up these resolutions in committee, to deal with it.
But before I take my seat, Mr. Speaker, .'here is a matter which I do not wish to treat at any length, but to which I would allude. My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) said this afternoon that we should have in this country a little more team play, and, probably to illustrate the thought that he had in his mind, he began and ended his speech with a few words in French. Now, Mr. Speaker, I too think that we should have a little more team play, and I would like to allude to that as a conclusion.
As a newly-elected member, fresh from my constituents, I would like to voice their feelings in this House and to express most sincerely the intense desire of my province for a good understanding with the Englishspeaking citizens of our country. This (may not be & matter exaetlv relevant to the Budget, hut I think it is closely connected with the general welfare of the country. During the war the province of Quebec was hmentably misrepresented, because people failed to understand the mentality of the French /Canadians; they attributed to enmity and to lack of loyalty and courage what was really a most normal and most explicable state of mind. This, of course, is a dead issue and I do not desire to revise it. But I may be permitted to rejoice in the fact that since the conclusion of the war a 'better account of my province is given in the press of the country, because in these times of stress and social strife the proper mentality of the French Canadian is better understood; the so-called "Quebec apathy" appears in its real significance and is properly branded as moderation, steadiness and love of the land. When the strikers ;n Winnipeg were hanging a thundering cloud over that western city; when Ontario cities-aye, Mr. Speaker, even the pure and holy Toronto-were threatening rebellion, the good old province of Quebec still re-

mained draped in its robe of quietness and peaceful stability. And the Montreal Star was well able to say:
If a red wave of Bolshevism should sweep from overseas, as some people fear, it would shatter itself upon Quebec's stability as the Atlantic surges are shattered on the Gasp6 cliffs.
I do say, Mr. Speaker-and I wish my hon. friends would well digest my words- that no province is more tolerant, more desirous for peace and harmony, than the province of Quebec. All that we demand- and it is treatment meted out to minorities within our borders-is a clear recognition of our rights; that is in full conformity; with the British spirit all over the world. Wherever the true British spirit has prevailed it has preserved the essentials of the nationalities over *which it has presided; .and that is the spirit that we wish to see flourish in Canada. The Confederation pact conferred on the two great Canadian races certain rights as to their schools, their language and their institutions. I again say, let us live not according to the letter, but according to the spirit of that pact. The letter of the law is cold, lifeless, and leads to much misunderstanding. As the dramatist says:
What damned error but some sober brow
Will bless it and approve it with a text?
But the spirit of the law is warm, peacebreathing, life-giving; and whenever these questions arise as to school or language, let us stand not by the cold interpretation, or, rather, falsification of the text, but by that high spiritual motive which animates the words and gives them their true light.
Again I deplore that this Budget is bringing nothing in the way of relief to the consumer from the heavy burden that he is now bearing, and that it has to admit such a lamentable situation so far as the condition of our financial affairs is concerned. The Government say that the country as a whole is prosperous and that the people are satisfied. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the kind of prosperity and satisfaction that the Canadian people are asking for and that they are entitled to? The Canadian people want prosperity, not a prosperity locked up in vaults, bank safes and cold storages, but a prosperity that will flow like the rays of the sun on every humble citizen of this Dominion. The Canadian people want peace-not a peace written in books or laws, enclosed in cryptograms which only few can decipher, but a peace that will live, that will rise and blossom in the hearts of every one. That peace,
that prosperity, the present Government have failed lamentably to bring about. They have had to face hard times and grave difficulties, but they have met them with a weak mind, an empty heart and a false purpose. And the Canadian people are longing for the time when it will be given them to elect new representatives and to choose a Government for this country more worthy of its great destiny and the gravity of the hour.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if it is not out of place, might I be permitted to observe-and I think I am voicing the opinion of hon. members on this side of the House-that there has been a distinct addition to the debating talent of this House by reason of the election for the constituency of St. James, of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Rinfret). I do not think that I can say that everybody agrees with all that he has said, but I desire to make these remarks, because my hon. friend and myself have been companions in arms in the past and I have a very friendly feeling towards, him anid I knew that if he ever came into this House, he would be able to hold his own in debate. I desired to pay this tribute to-night before commencing to make the remarks I intend to offer on the Budget.
First of all, I am going to pay this tribute to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), that he was at least heroic and courageous in the Budget which he introduced, and I am not going to offer any serious objections to his taxation proposals, because I am one who, I think, during the time I have been in this House, has consistently advocated the removal of certain forms of taxation. But I realized all along that if J advocated those things and they came about, we had to introduce another form of taxation, and that form of taxation had to he direct. I might criticise the expenditure that has been made by this Government and the previous Government. I might say that this Government is not practising economy as it should practise it; but I must realize this fact that Canada to-day has very heavy financial obligations, and it is the duty of Canada to meet those obligations, and the duty of this Parliament in some form or other to adopt means of taxtion that will raise the necessary money for that purpose.
During the war I think we should have imposed greater taxation upon the people, because I feel that many people, during that period, were better able to pay taxes to this country than some of them are at the present time. If we had done that, we

might have been able t-o face the period after the commencement of peace with a much smaller debt than we have now. At any rate these proposals have been made for the purpose of meeting our financial obligations, and as long as the money that is raised by this taxation goes toward that purpose, I am prepared to support that taxation, although I must confess that I agree with some of the criticisms which have been offered, that in some instances, at any rate, these proposals do not hit at luxuries but at actual necessities-. But where these taxes hit at actual luxuries, I am in favour of them and am prepared to defend them.
All of us, I suppose, cry for economy in the administration of the affairs of the country, but I find that most of us contradict ourselves by frequently placing before the Government claims for the expenditure of money. It is our duty at this time to demand only absolutely necessary expenditure upon those things that will be helpful to the development of this Dominion, and we should refrain from expenditures upon what we can safely call unnecessary things.
It is not my intention tq make a lengthy speech, but- I feel it is my duty as a member of this House to state clearly and distinctly my views on the tariff proposals contained in the Budget. I am quite in -accord with the attitude the Government have taken in removing the war taxes. The more of these taxes they remove, the more I shall be inclined to favour the Government; but at the same time I feel I aan standing to-night at the parting of the ways as regards my views in connection with the tariff, and I want to give my reasons foT my -stand along that line. Ever since I came into this House I have been a supporter of a low tariff; I have never at any time advocated free trade; nor have I at any time advocated moderate protection; but I thought, and I still think, that the reasonable policy to advocate is a low tariff and a tariff directed primarily for the raising of revenue and not -for the purpose of protecting industries in this country. That is still my view and 1 want to be consistent with my record in the past in directing the course I intend to take ias regards the Budget at this time. I -might be able to support the taxation proposals, but it has been made clear to me during this debate that whatever revision of the tariff is to come is to be a revision that is going to maintain protection; and I would be inclined -to say that the moderate protection that is being advocated really means high protection, because I have here the words of the Minister of

Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Balla-ntyne) in quoting the increased tariff in Australia. The minister made this observation, after quoting the items;
That will serve to show what our sister Dominion is doing. Australia evidently believes in a policy of moderate protection.
And the items that the minister was quoting >n regard to Australia showed that Australia was increasing its tariff. Consequently, if moderate piotection means an increase in the tariff, I cannot be in sympathy with moderate protection. I do not think this Government looks to a man to support them through thick and thin on every policy they introduce. I was not elected to this House under any such consideration. When I appealed to the people of my crnstituency in 1917, I told them that I was standing for a war policy and a war Government; and when I was asked where I stood on the tariff, I told them that I stood where I had always stood, namely, in favour of a low tariff and I did not intend to 'ary my position in that regard, but tbal I did not think the tariff should l-e any c nnsideration daring the war and it was my intention to support Union Government And I did so during the period of war. But as I said ;n speaking on the Address at the opening of this session, I felt that as regards the tariff and other domestic policies, I was free to act in the way that I considered to be in the best interests of the country and in accord with the course I had always followed on this particular question.
Coming to a consideration of the Budget, I might say this, that the points the amendment aims at I am in sympathy with. Anything that will tend to reduce the cost of living cr anything that will tend to encourage pioduction in this country has my support and sympathy, and I feel that a reduction in the tariff aims in those directions. Why, I have the words of my good friend1 the Minister of Marine and Fisheries-anid he is -my good friend, although 1 cannot agree wth him in his views on the tariff-that the removal of the war tax of 7i per cent will tend io reduce the cost of living. When he was speaking on the Budget he stated, that tie accusation of the hon. imemiber for Brome (Mr. MeMaster) that this Government had not done anything to reduce the cost of living was untrue, because fhe removal of the 7i per cent war tax will lessen the cost ot living, let us i educe the tariff still *'u rther on the necessaries oi life, and thus further reduce the

cost of living. That is my stand on the tariff
As to the whole question of protection, I do not want to see any industry in this country driven out of business. I have -been told time and again, and I have heard it claimed on the floor of this House, that protection was primarily intended for the infant industries of this country. Now I might be influenced to support -protection if it was for that purpose; but when I find that the industries of this country have been in the Infants' Home practically from 1878 until the present time, I reach the conclusion that the industries never pass the infantile stage, they are in that stage always. Now I do feel this, that our industries in this country should be well enough organized and should be able to put by sufficient reserves, after a period of protection, in order to face outside competition. They should not expect protection for all time to come, and I think the time is ripe now to cut away a great deal of that protection.
In regard to the question of the development of our natural resources and their connection with the tariff, I have urged this matter on previous occasions, and I urge it again now, that i: by the removal of the tariff we can make the implements of production cheaper and thereby encourage the development of our natural resources we are doing something worth while for this country. It is the development of our natural resources that we desire at the present time because the development of those resources will enrich Canada and enable it to meet its pressing obligations. What do I find in the province of Alberta? Men are going out, individuals and companies, and spending thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars in an effort to find oil in that province. But practically everything they use in the operations to discover oil is taxed. Now I do not think in a case of that kind, vrfhere there is an attempt to develop our natural resources, and where if oil was found it would mean millions of dollars to this country, that those implements should be taxed any more than the implements used by the farmers who also are engaged in the development of our natural resources. I have a case in point, a local one, which I should like to give in this connection. In the section of Alberta from which flj come many acres are devoted to the production of Alfalfa. Except for an exceptional year like last year when there was a shortage of feed throughout Western Canada I would say that there
was a surplus of alfalfa produced in that section, and men who realize that with the development of. irrigation there is going to be a large increase in the alfalfa area are looking for some other purpose to use that alfalfa. An enterprising gentleman in my , constituency decided he would go into the alfalfa milling business in order to produce a meal that could be used for stock feeding. He wrote to me wanting to find out whether he could get a certain machine for -that particular purpose into Canada free of duty. It was -a machine that was not produced in Canada and was for -the purpose of utilizing one of our own resources and making it profitable, and encouraging the development of the alfalfa area on irrigated land. This particular machine, an alfalfa grinder, valued at about $4,000, I found, was subject to a duty of 20 per cent, or nearly $800. That was a tax on what I would call a productive implement necessary for the development of our resources in Western Canada.
Briefly I feel, as I indicated before, that whatever revision of the tariff is contemplated is to be along the lines of protection. And when we speak of moderate protection I would say that it means sufficient protection at least to satisfy the industries of this country, and I have not yet been converted to the view that adequate protection or moderate protection for protection's sake only is desirable in this country. Consequently, under these circumstances, I cannot commit myself to a proposition inconsistent with the atttiude I have taken in this House from the beginning. I feel therefore it is my duty to go on record now as being in favour of a reduction of the tariff, and for that reason I intend to support the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding).
Before taking my seat I would like to point out to the Government a matter that I think is worthy of some attention, and again it is a case which comes from the section of the country which I represent, but I think it is important to the whole country. We are very anxious to develop our export trade and I think it should be -the business of this Government-I am not complaining that they are not pursuing this policy-to widen our markets all over the *world, and wherever we can get a footing in a new market we should get it, and get it as soon as possible. I feel that on the Pacific we have opportunities for the development of a great deal of trade with Canada if we only keep our eyes open and get after that trade. We did have a trade in flour

with Hong Kong, and I think it is worth mentioning that one mill alone in the city where I live exported in 1912 to Hong Kong and Shanghai 155,901 bags of flour, in 1913, 182,404 bags of flour and in 1914, 101,196 bags of flour. When the war broke out that market dropped until there was practically nothing shipped in the other years. I am told by millers at the present time it is practically impossible to get into that market, by reason of an order of the Wheat Board. The Wheat Board says it will only issue a permit to ship to Hong Kong on receipt of a regular application form, accompanied by a cheque for $2 a barrel refund to the board. The millers claim that the $2 a barrel refund demand practically keeps them out of that Oriental market. It may surprise the House to know how much flour has been shipped from Australia to fHong Kong and Shanghai. The importer who writes this letter in the correspondence that has been submitted to me says that practically all this market is open to Canada and could be used by Canada at the .present time. He says:
Yet in spite of all the difficulties, shipping and so forth, this market (the Hong Kong market) imported 1,200,000 bags of Australian flour last year and will probably continue importing large quantities.
What I want to point out is this : Seemingly from this order of our Wheat Board we are unable to ship flour to Hong Kong in competition with other countries and we .are losing a market we formerly had. Now I am not in a position to condemn offhand the Wheat Board. There is a great difference of opinion as to the Wheat Board. I am not a farmer or a miller, but it seems to me that in this case that particular policy is not in the interests of the milling trade of Canada any more than it is in the interests of the export trade of Canada, and this situation should be remedied if we want to build up with the Pacific countries a large export trade.
I have attempted to outline as briefly as possible my views on the Budget. I might ,say again that I am merely attempting to be consistent with the course that I have always taken on the tariff. I have noticed [DOT]during this debate that there has been some criticism of other hon. members for their lack of consistency. Well, I may be inconsistent on some other questions, but on [DOT]the tariff I think I can claim I have always been consistent, and it is merely to be consistent, and to continue to be consistent [DOT]until I am enlightened that I am wrong, that I am taking the course I have announced to-night.

/Mr. Speaker, the Budget 'Speech of this session of 1920 should have been made by the Finance Minister of ,a new Government created by the popular will on an economic platform, duly submitted to the Canadian people, for the purpose of purifying our finances and developing our country after the war. But such is not the 176
case and the Government we have opposite ds ever the same Government that juggled away the 1917 elections, through their ignominous Election Act and their cry of " Win the War."
Well, now the war is over, it has been won, and the Win-the-war Government still clings tiCi power instead of going before the electorate to give an account of its war policy and obtaining from them a new mandate for a policy of peace and of national reconstruction.
The Union Government shuns the day of its rendering of accounts. The Minister of Finance has indeed produced his balance-sheet, but only in this House, where he is assured of a majority, the Government dare not go before the people and submit to it the deeds, or rather the misdeeds, of their administration, for they are well aware of the people's answer. The Government shun their responsibilities; it is one of the features of their character, or to state it in a better form, it is a sure indication of their lack of character.
'Since 1914, the . Government have appointed more than 100 commissioners to do what they should have performed themselves, and yet we had 26 different ministers, a figure that had never been reached previously; in spite of all that commissions have followed upon commissions, subcorn-missions upon suboommissions, without as a rule reaching any solution at all. Every time the Government entrusted any question to a special commission, the said question was sure of a first-class funeral. God knows how many serious questions the Unionist Government have thus solemnly buried! The Government shun their responsibilities. They have proved it by ever shifting to some other party the trouble c.f looking up matters they should have settled themselves, thereby leaving without any remedy all the evils which the Canadian people were then, and are still suffering.
'.I shall not undertake to enumerate the numberless commissions created by the Government since 1914 in order to shirk their responsibilities. The most important is, beyond a doubt, the Board of Oonrmeree which should have assisted in the lowering of the cost of living. Well, since this Board has been appointed, the cost of living has daily increased. The cold storage plants- it has been stated many a time-.are crammed with foodstuffs; the profits of numerous profiteers are scandalous, the profits of certain tradesmen are exorbitant,
